name: Quality of Service (QoS)
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Explain QoS per-hop behavior: marking with CoS and DSCP, trust boundaries, LLQ and CBWFQ, WRED, policing and shaping.

resources.title: Free CCNA 200-301 course (Jeremy's IT Lab)

resources.title: Compare Traffic Policing and Traffic Shaping to Limit Bandwidth

resources.title: Implement QoS Policies with Differentiated Services Code Point

resources.title: RFC 4594: Configuration Guidelines for DiffServ Service Classes

lesson.intro: When a link congests, something must wait and something may be dropped, and QoS decides which. The CCNA asks you to explain the per-hop behavior: classify and mark, trust, queue, avoid congestion, police and shape.
objectives: Describe bandwidth, delay, jitter and loss and what voice, video and data need
Explain marking with CoS, IP Precedence and DSCP, including EF, AF and CS
Place a trust boundary and explain why endpoint markings are not trusted
Compare CBWFQ and LLQ, tail drop and WRED, and policing and shaping
Read a class-map and policy-map exhibit and trace a voice packet hop by hop

sections.title: Why QoS: congestion, delay, jitter and loss
sections.key: QoS decides who waits and who is dropped when a link congests; it adds no bandwidth. Voice needs at most 150 ms delay, 30 ms jitter and 1 percent loss.
sections.body:
At 9 a.m. a 40 GB backup fills a branch's 100 Mbps WAN link and the manager's video call stutters. Nothing is broken: packets wait in a queue, and when it is full they are dropped. **Quality of Service (QoS)** decides who waits and who gets dropped.

[[visual]]

Applications need very different things:

[[visual 2]]

A resent syllable would arrive too late, so voice rides on UDP and simply suffers the loss.

**QoS does not create bandwidth**: on an uncongested link it has nothing to do.

The CCNA uses the **DiffServ** model: each device decides per packet, a **per-hop behavior (PHB)**, from its classification and marking. With no end-to-end reservation, consistent policies at every hop make QoS work end to end.

rows: Capacity available to a flow, in bits per second
Time from sender to receiver, usually one way
Variation in delay between consecutive packets: 100 ms then 300 ms means the listener hears a gap
Share of packets that never arrive

visual.caption: Video figures as quoted in the official guide; interactive video is usually handled like voice.

sections.tip: Voice numbers to memorize: 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter, 1 percent loss.
sections.pitfall: Thinking QoS adds capacity. It only rations what exists; a link that is overloaded all day needs more bandwidth, not more QoS.

check.question: Which characteristic describes the variation in delay between consecutive packets of a voice call?
choices: Latency
Jitter
Loss
Bandwidth
check.explanation: Jitter is the variation in one-way delay from packet to packet. Latency is the delay itself, loss is packets that never arrive and bandwidth is capacity. Voice tolerates at most about 30 ms of jitter.

sections.title: Classification and marking
sections.key: Classify once near the source, then mark. CoS (3 bits, 802.1Q tag) is lost at the first router; DSCP (6 bits, IP header) lasts end to end.
sections.body:
To treat voice better than a backup, a device must know which packet is which. **Classification** matches packets on the incoming interface, an ACL (addresses and ports), existing markings, or **NBAR2**, which recognizes thousands of applications by looking deeper than an ACL can.

Classifying in detail at every hop would be slow. So classify carefully **once**, close to the source, and **mark** the packet in a header field reserved for QoS. Later devices just read the marking.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

A packet from an IP phone may leave with CoS 5 in its 802.1Q tag and DSCP EF in its IP header. The CoS disappears at the first router, which builds a new frame; the DSCP survives to the far end.

visual.title: IPv4 ToS byte (DS field): DSCP lives here

rows.label: DSCP, first 3 bits = old IP Precedence

visual.caption: DSCP is the first 6 bits; IP Precedence used only the first 3. IPv6 carries the same bits in its Traffic Class byte.

rows: Only on tagged links: trunks, voice VLAN

sections.tip: Classify once near the source, then mark; every later device just reads the DSCP.
sections.pitfall: Relying on CoS for end-to-end QoS. CoS lives in the 802.1Q tag, so it is lost as soon as a router forwards the packet onto another link.

check.question: A packet crosses two switch trunks, a router and a WAN link. Which marking stays with it the whole way?
choices: CoS
TID
EXP
DSCP
check.explanation: DSCP sits in the IP header, which routers forward intact, so it lasts end to end. CoS exists only in the 802.1Q tag on trunk links, TID only on Wi-Fi and EXP only inside an MPLS network.

sections.title: DSCP values: EF, AF and CS
sections.key: EF (46) marks voice. AFxy = 8x + 2y, and a higher y is dropped sooner. CSx = 8x, and CS0 (DSCP 0) is best effort.
sections.body:
The DiffServ RFCs suggest standard DSCP values. Three families matter.

**Expedited Forwarding (EF), DSCP 46**: low delay, jitter and loss, in practice **voice payload**. Cisco IP phones mark voice EF and call signaling CS3.

**Assured Forwarding, AFxy**: class x (1 to 4) shares one queue, and y (1 to 3) is the **drop precedence**: a higher y is dropped **sooner**, so AF43 goes before AF41. The value is **8x + 2y**.

[[visual]]

**Class Selector, CS0 to CS7**: kept for IP Precedence compatibility, so **CSx = 8x** (CS3 = 24, CS6 = 48). **CS0 (DSCP 0) is default, best-effort traffic.**

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: The six DSCP bits
visual.caption: The first three bits equal IP Precedence: EF's 101 is IPP 5, the old voice value. CS values always end in three zeros.

sections.tip: A capture may show the whole ToS byte. Drop the two ECN bits: 0xB8 = 101110 00 = EF (46), 0x88 = 100010 00 = AF41 (34).
sections.pitfall: Getting AF drop precedence backwards. A higher second digit means more likely to be dropped: AF43 goes before AF41.

activity.title: DSCP values in binary
activity.prompt: DSCP is a 6-bit number. Before the drill, build 46 (EF), 34 (AF41) and 24 (CS3) in the low six bits and compare the patterns: CS values always end in three zeros, and in an AF value the class number sits in the top three of the six bits. Then hit the five targets.

check.question: Within the AF3 class, which marking is dropped first when congestion avoidance starts discarding packets?
choices: AF33
AF31
AF32
All three are dropped equally
check.explanation: The second digit is the drop precedence, and higher means dropped sooner. AF33 (DSCP 30) goes first, then AF32, while AF31 is protected longest. They share a queue but not the same drop treatment.

sections.title: Trust boundaries
sections.key: A trust boundary is where markings start being trusted. Put it on a device IT controls: the access switch port, or a Cisco IP phone with a PC behind it.
sections.body:
A user reads that voice gets priority and sets their PC to mark every packet DSCP 46. If the network believed it, downloads would land in the voice queue and real calls would suffer.

So a network defines a **trust boundary**: markings from beyond it are ignored or rewritten, and markings from inside it are honored. It belongs as close to the source as possible, on a device IT controls.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Inside the boundary, every switch and router reads the DSCP and applies its policy: fast matching on one field instead of repeating complex classification. Providers do the same at their own edge, re-marking or policing customer traffic to the classes the contract pays for.

items.title: PC on an access port
points: The switch classifies and re-marks as traffic enters, often to DSCP 0 unless an ACL or NBAR rule says otherwise

items.title: IP phone with a PC behind it
points: The phone is trusted: the boundary moves to the phone
It marks its own voice CoS 5 and DSCP EF
It re-marks the PC's traffic to a low value (typically CoS 0)
Conditional trust: the switch extends trust only when CDP detects a Cisco phone

sections.tip: Trust what IT controls: phones and network devices yes, user PCs no.
sections.pitfall: Trusting markings on every access port. Any user who sets DSCP EF on a PC then competes with real voice in the priority queue.

check.question: A Cisco IP phone connects to an access switch and a PC is plugged into the phone. Where is the trust boundary usually placed?
choices: At the PC, because it originates the traffic
At the WAN router, where congestion happens
At the IP phone
At the core switch
check.explanation: The phone is a device IT controls, sits closest to the source and re-marks the PC's traffic, so it is the natural trust boundary. The PC is never trusted, and pushing trust back to the WAN or core would leave earlier hops acting on unverified markings.

sections.title: Queuing: CBWFQ and LLQ
sections.key: CBWFQ guarantees each class a minimum share of the link; LLQ adds a priority queue that is always served first but is policed to its configured bandwidth.
sections.body:
In a single **FIFO** queue, voice waits behind every backup packet ahead of it. A queuing system has three parts:

[[visual]]

**CBWFQ (Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing)** is a weighted round robin: each class gets **at least** its share during congestion. Fine for data, but a voice packet that just missed its turn waits for the other queues, which adds delay and jitter.

**LLQ (Low Latency Queuing)** adds a **priority queue** to CBWFQ that the scheduler always serves first. To prevent **queue starvation** of the others, the priority queue has a built-in **policer**: its bandwidth is a **maximum** during congestion, and the excess is dropped. Size it for the expected calls.

[[visual 2]]

A common design: voice and interactive video in priority queues, business data in CBWFQ classes, the rest in the default class:

[[code]]

steps.label: Classifier sorts packets into queues by marking
Scheduler picks which queue sends next

items.title: CBWFQ class
points: May use more when the link is free
Served in turn: can add delay and jitter

items.title: LLQ priority queue
points: Always served first: almost no delay, jitter or loss

sections.code:
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any VIDEO
 match dscp af41
!
policy-map WAN-EDGE
 class VOICE
  priority percent 20
 class VIDEO
  bandwidth percent 30
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 service-policy output WAN-EDGE
sections.tip: CBWFQ guarantees a minimum share. LLQ's priority queue guarantees low delay but is capped at its configured bandwidth.
sections.pitfall: Putting bulk data in the priority queue to make it faster. The priority queue's policer drops the excess, and the traffic that truly needs low delay suffers.

check.question: Why is CBWFQ on its own not ideal for voice?
choices: CBWFQ cannot guarantee any bandwidth to a class
A round-robin scheduler can still make voice packets wait their turn, adding delay and jitter
CBWFQ drops all UDP traffic during congestion
CBWFQ only works on trunk links that carry CoS
check.explanation: CBWFQ guarantees a minimum share but still serves queues in turn, so a voice packet may wait while other queues are served. LLQ fixes this with a priority queue that always goes first. CBWFQ does guarantee bandwidth and works on any interface.

sections.title: Congestion avoidance: tail drop and WRED
sections.key: Tail drop discards every new packet once a queue is full, causing TCP global synchronization; WRED drops a few TCP packets early, starting with higher drop precedence.
sections.body:
When a queue is full, every new packet for it is discarded: **tail drop**, whatever its importance. TCP makes it worse, because a sender cuts its rate sharply after a loss:

[[visual]]

**Congestion avoidance** drops a few packets early, before the queue fills, so only some TCP senders slow down at a time. Cisco's tool is **WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection)**, which watches the **average queue depth**:

[[visual 2]]

The **weighted** part uses the markings: higher AF drop precedence (AF13) starts dropping earlier and harder than AF11 in the same queue.

WRED relies on TCP backing off. UDP voice does not slow down after a drop, so early drops only hurt calls: one more reason voice lives in the priority queue. Keep the families apart: queuing decides the **order** packets leave; congestion avoidance decides **which** to drop as a queue fills.

visual.title: TCP global synchronization

steps.label: A full queue tail-drops packets from hundreds of TCP flows at once
All the senders cut their rate together
All the senders speed up together and overflow the queue again

visual.loop: The sawtooth repeats: wasted bandwidth and loss

layers.label: Above the maximum threshold
layers.detail: Every new packet is dropped, like tail drop

layers.label: Between minimum and maximum
layers.detail: A random, rising share is dropped (say up to 10%)

sections.pitfall: Applying WRED to voice. Voice uses UDP, which does not slow down after a drop, so early drops only damage call quality.

check.question: What problem is WRED mainly designed to avoid?
choices: Voice packets waiting behind data packets
Packets being marked incorrectly at the access layer
A link carrying more than its contracted rate
Many TCP flows losing packets at once from tail drop and slowing down together
check.explanation: WRED drops a few TCP packets early and at random so flows back off at different times, avoiding the mass tail drops behind TCP global synchronization. Voice waiting is solved by LLQ, wrong markings by a trust boundary and contract rates by shaping or policing.

sections.title: Policing versus shaping
sections.key: Both enforce a rate. A policer drops or re-marks the excess (loss, no delay, usually inbound); a shaper queues it and sends it later (delay, egress only).
sections.body:
Your WAN service arrives on a 1 Gbps port, but the contract, the **CIR** (committed information rate), is 200 Mbps. Two tools enforce a rate; the difference is what they do with the excess:

[[visual]]

The provider **polices** your traffic at 200 Mbps as it enters their network. You **shape** your outbound traffic to 200 Mbps so their policer never has to drop anything. Both allow short **bursts** above the rate after a quiet period.

Shaping has a catch for voice. A shaper sends at full line rate for part of each interval (**Tc**) and then pauses:

[[visual 2]]

A shaper creates a queue, so run LLQ and CBWFQ inside it. The typical WAN edge: classify and mark at the access edge, trust inside the boundary, then shape on egress with LLQ and CBWFQ inside and WRED on the data queues.

visual.title: Shaping 200 Mbps on a 1 Gbps link

steps.label: A voice packet arrives in the pause
steps.work:
waits up to 800 ms
budget is 150 ms

visual.result: Cisco recommends a 10 ms Tc when voice or video is present

sections.tip: Police drops, shape delays. Providers police at the CIR; customers shape to the CIR.
sections.pitfall: Saying that policing buffers traffic. It never queues: the excess is dropped or re-marked at once. Shaping is the one that buffers.

check.question: An enterprise router sends to a provider that drops all traffic above a 50 Mbps CIR. Which tool should the enterprise apply outbound on its WAN interface?
choices: Shaping to 50 Mbps
Policing to 50 Mbps
WRED with a 50 Mbps threshold
Marking all traffic CS0
check.explanation: Shaping queues the excess and releases it at 50 Mbps, so the provider's policer has nothing to drop. Policing on the customer side would just drop the traffic earlier, WRED manages queue depth rather than rate, and re-marking changes priority, not rate.

sections.title: Reading a QoS policy: class maps, policy maps and service-policy
sections.key: In MQC a class-map classifies, a policy-map acts on each class, and service-policy attaches it in one direction. Queuing and shaping work only on output.
sections.body:
Cisco IOS expresses QoS with the **Modular QoS CLI (MQC)**. The CCNA does not ask you to write it, but exhibits show it:

[[visual]]

On the access switch, a policy such as MARK-IN (`service-policy input`) is the trust boundary at work: it matches a softphone with an ACL and runs `set dscp ef`, and sets everything else to `set dscp default` (0), whatever the PC marked.

The WAN router in the exhibit shapes all traffic to the 50 Mbps contract and runs a **child policy** inside the shaper. The shaper creates the queue; the child decides who leaves first. Child percentages are shares of the shaped 50 Mbps, not of the 1 Gbps interface.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

Read any policy the same way: start at service-policy and its direction, follow the policy map, and for each class name the tool: classification, marking, queuing, congestion avoidance, policing or shaping.

rows: Classification: `match dscp ef`, `match access-group name VOICE-ACL`, `match protocol` (NBAR). `match-any` needs one line to match; `match-all`, the default, needs every line

Actions per class: `set dscp` marks, `priority` is the LLQ queue, `bandwidth` a CBWFQ minimum, `random-detect dscp-based` WRED, `police` drops or re-marks, `shape average` queues. `class class-default` catches the rest
Attaches a policy to an interface. Marking and policing work either way; queuing and shaping only on **output**, because a device can only schedule packets it is about to send

sections.code:
! WAN router: shape to the contract, queue inside the shaper
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any VIDEO
 match dscp af41
policy-map WAN-QUEUE
 class VOICE
  priority percent 20
 class VIDEO
  bandwidth percent 30
 class class-default
  bandwidth percent 25
  random-detect dscp-based
policy-map WAN-OUT
 class class-default
  shape average 50000000
  service-policy WAN-QUEUE
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 service-policy output WAN-OUT
sections.tip: Read MQC from the outside in: service-policy and its direction, then the policy-map, then each class-map.
sections.pitfall: Attaching a queuing or shaping policy with service-policy input. Queues exist only on output, and IOS refuses priority, bandwidth and shape in an input policy.

check.question: In the exhibit, what does the WAN router do with VIDEO traffic during congestion?
choices: Sends it before voice, because video needs more bandwidth
Guarantees it at least 30 percent of the shaped 50 Mbps, about 15 Mbps
Caps it at 30 percent of the 1 Gbps interface
Re-marks it AF41 before queuing it
check.explanation: bandwidth percent 30 is a CBWFQ minimum, and in a child policy under a shaper the percentage applies to the shaped rate, so video gets at least 15 Mbps when the link is busy and may use more when it is not. Voice, in the priority queue, still goes first. The class matches packets already marked AF41; it does not mark them.

sections.title: One voice packet, hop by hop
sections.key: Marking happens once at the edge and trust is decided at the first switch; every later hop queues, shapes or polices by reading the DSCP.
sections.body:
Follow one packet of a phone call from a branch to headquarters, next to one packet of a file backup on the same path:

[[visual]]

The voice budget is 150 ms one way. Each priority queue costs only a few milliseconds, and the 10 ms Tc keeps the shaper's pause short. The backup absorbs the waiting and the occasional early drop, and TCP quietly resends. That is QoS in one sentence: not more bandwidth, but a deliberate decision about who waits.

Exam questions often hide one broken hop: an untrusted marking reset to 0 at the access switch, voice in a CBWFQ class instead of the priority queue, WRED on voice, or a shaper with a long Tc. Walk the hops in order and the fault stands out.

rows: Marked DSCP EF and CoS 5 on the voice VLAN
PC traffic re-marked to 0 by the phone
Trusts the Cisco phone: EF stands
Its own policy would set 0 anyway
Priority queue by DSCP (and CoS on trunks), no reclassifying
Shaper at 50 Mbps with 10 ms Tc; LLQ sends it next, within 20%
Waits in class-default; WRED may drop a few TCP segments early
Policed at the CIR but conforms, since the branch shaped. EF can map to MPLS EXP
The same per-hop treatment to the far phone

sections.tip: Classify and mark once at the edge; every later hop queues, avoids congestion, shapes and polices by reading the marking.
sections.pitfall: Configuring QoS only on the WAN router. Every hop that can congest needs a consistent policy, or the packet loses its priority wherever the policy is missing.

check.question: In the walk-through, why does the provider's policer drop nothing from the branch?
choices: Voice is marked EF, and policers never drop EF traffic
WRED on the branch router removes all the excess first
The branch router shapes its output to the contracted rate before the provider sees it
Policers only act on TCP traffic
check.explanation: Shaping at the branch queues the excess and releases it at the CIR, so the traffic reaching the provider already conforms. A policer drops or re-marks anything above its rate regardless of marking, WRED only manages queue depth, and policers measure all traffic in their class, TCP or not.

keyTerms.definition: The DiffServ idea that each device independently treats a packet according to its classification and marking.
Variation in one-way delay between consecutive packets. Voice tolerates about 30 ms.
Identifying traffic (by interface, ACL, NBAR or existing markings) and writing a QoS value into a header so later devices can act on it.
Class of Service: 3 bits (PCP) in the 802.1Q tag, values 0 to 7, present only on tagged links.
Differentiated Services Code Point: the first 6 bits of the IP ToS/DS byte, 64 values, carried end to end.
Expedited Forwarding, DSCP 46: low delay, jitter and loss, used for voice payload.
Assured Forwarding: class x (1 to 4) and drop precedence y (1 to 3), value 8x + 2y. Higher y is dropped sooner.
The point where a network starts trusting QoS markings, ideally the access switch port or an IP phone.
Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing: weighted round robin that guarantees each class a minimum share during congestion.
Low Latency Queuing: CBWFQ plus a strict priority queue, capped by a built-in policer, for voice and interactive video.
Weighted Random Early Detection: drops a random share of packets between a minimum and maximum queue depth, more aggressively for higher drop precedence.
Both enforce a rate. Policing drops or re-marks the excess; shaping queues it and sends it later, egress only.
Modular QoS CLI: class-map classifies, policy-map assigns actions to each class, and service-policy input or output applies the policy to an interface.
Committed information rate: the traffic rate a provider contracts to carry, enforced by its policer and matched by the customer's shaper.
The time interval a shaper uses to meter traffic. Cisco recommends 10 ms when voice or video crosses the shaper.

summary: QoS acts only during congestion; voice needs 150 ms delay, 30 ms jitter, 1 percent loss or less.
Classify once near the source and mark; later hops apply a per-hop behavior from the marking.
CoS (3 bits, 802.1Q) lives on trunks; DSCP (6 bits) lasts end to end. EF 46, AFxy = 8x + 2y, CSx = 8x.
Trust markings only from devices IT controls: the access switch port or a Cisco IP phone.
CBWFQ guarantees minimums; LLQ adds a capped priority queue for voice; WRED drops TCP early.
Policing drops or re-marks the excess; shaping queues it and adds delay, egress only.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why their video call breaks up when someone else in the house starts a huge download, and how a router with QoS (marking, a priority queue and shaping) could keep the call smooth without adding any bandwidth.

questions.question: What does QoS do on a link that is never congested?
choices: It doubles the usable bandwidth
Practically nothing, because no packets have to wait
It encrypts the voice traffic
It keeps dropping low-priority traffic
questions.explanation: QoS tools act when packets must queue. If the link always has room, every packet leaves immediately and the scheduler has no choices to make. QoS never adds bandwidth.

questions.question: Match each traffic characteristic to its meaning.

pairs.right: Capacity available, in bits per second
Time for a packet to travel from sender to receiver
Variation in delay between consecutive packets
Share of packets that never arrive

questions.explanation: QoS manages these four. Voice is the most demanding on delay, jitter and loss, while bulk data mostly cares about bandwidth.

questions.question: Which set of targets matches Cisco's guidance for interactive voice?
choices: One-way delay 400 ms, jitter 100 ms, loss 5% or less
One-way delay 15 ms, jitter 3 ms, loss 0.01% or less
One-way delay 150 ms, jitter 30 ms, loss 1% or less
Round-trip delay 1 second, any jitter, loss 10% or less
questions.explanation: The figures to remember for voice are 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter and 1 percent loss. Beyond those, calls become noticeably poor.

questions.question: Why does voice traffic use UDP instead of relying on TCP retransmission?
choices: A retransmitted voice packet would arrive too late to be useful
UDP has a larger maximum payload
TCP cannot carry real-time traffic across routers
UDP packets are automatically marked EF
questions.explanation: Speech has to be played in real time; a syllable resent half a second later is useless. So voice accepts a little loss instead. UDP does not mark packets by itself; marking is a QoS action.

questions.question: What does per-hop behavior (PHB) mean in the DiffServ QoS model?
choices: The first router reserves bandwidth along the whole path before a call starts
Only the last hop applies QoS before delivery
Every hop must use identical queue sizes
Each device independently treats a packet according to its classification and marking
questions.explanation: In DiffServ there is no end-to-end reservation. Every router and switch applies its own policy to each packet, usually by reading the DSCP marking, so consistent policies at each hop produce end-to-end QoS.

questions.question: How many bits long is the DSCP field?
questions.explanation: DSCP is the first 6 bits of the IPv4 ToS byte (the DS field), giving 64 values. IP Precedence and CoS are 3 bits, and 12 bits is the VLAN ID.

questions.question: Where is the CoS marking carried?
choices: In the IPv4 header's ToS byte
In the TCP header
In the 802.1Q tag of an Ethernet frame
In the MPLS label
questions.explanation: CoS (PCP) is 3 bits in the 802.1Q tag, so it exists only on tagged links. The ToS byte carries IPP and DSCP, and MPLS has its own EXP bits.

questions.question: Which two statements about CoS and DSCP are true? (Choose two.)
choices: DSCP stays with the packet across routed hops
CoS is lost when a router forwards the packet onto a new link
CoS has 64 possible values
DSCP exists only on 802.1Q trunks
CoS is carried in the IP header
questions.explanation: DSCP is in the IP header and survives routing. CoS is in the 802.1Q tag, which a router removes when it builds a new frame. CoS has 8 values, not 64.

questions.question: Which tool lets a router classify traffic by application, beyond the addresses and ports an ACL can match?
choices: WRED
LLQ
CDP
NBAR
questions.explanation: NBAR (now NBAR2) recognizes applications by inspecting traffic more deeply than an ACL. WRED and LLQ act on traffic after it is classified, and CDP is a discovery protocol.

questions.question: What is the decimal DSCP value of EF (Expedited Forwarding)?
questions.explanation: EF is DSCP 46, binary 101110, the standard marking for voice payload.

questions.question: What is the decimal DSCP value of AF31?
questions.explanation: AFxy = 8x + 2y, so AF31 = 8 x 3 + 2 x 1 = 26.

questions.question: Match each marking to its DSCP decimal value.
questions.explanation: AFxy = 8x + 2y and CSx = 8x. EF is 46. CS0 (DSCP 0) is best effort.

questions.question: Order these markings from least likely to most likely to be dropped by WRED when their shared queue fills.
questions.explanation: They share the AF2 queue; the second digit is drop precedence, and a higher value is dropped earlier.

questions.question: Order these markings by their DSCP decimal value, lowest first.
questions.explanation: CS0 = 0, AF11 = 10, CS3 = 24, AF41 = 34, EF = 46, CS6 = 48. Use AFxy = 8x + 2y and CSx = 8x.

questions.question: A packet arrives marked DSCP 36. Which per-hop behavior name is that?
choices: AF41
AF42
AF33
CS4
questions.explanation: 36 = 8 x 4 + 2 x 2, so x = 4 and y = 2: AF42. AF41 is 34, AF33 is 30 and CS4 is 32.

questions.question: Which DSCP marking does a Cisco IP phone use by default for voice payload?
choices: CS3
AF41
EF
CS0
questions.explanation: Voice payload is marked EF (46). The phone marks call signaling CS3, AF41 is typically interactive video and CS0 is best effort.

questions.question: A packet capture on the WAN link shows the exhibit. What is this packet most likely carrying, and where should an LLQ policy put it?
questions.code:
Internet Protocol Version 4, Src: 10.1.10.25, Dst: 10.9.0.40
    Differentiated Services Field: 0xb8 (DSCP: EF, ECN: Not-ECT)
        1011 10.. = Differentiated Services Codepoint: Expedited Forwarding (46)
    Total Length: 200
User Datagram Protocol, Src Port: 16384, Dst Port: 24580
choices: Interactive video, in a CBWFQ class with guaranteed bandwidth
Best-effort data, in class-default
Call signaling, in the priority queue
Voice payload, in the priority queue
questions.explanation: DSCP 46 is EF, and 0xb8 is just the whole ToS byte (101110 followed by the two ECN bits). Small UDP packets marked EF are voice payload, which belongs in the LLQ priority queue. Call signaling is CS3 and interactive video AF41.

questions.question: A user sets their PC to mark all traffic DSCP EF. The access switch port is outside the trust boundary. What happens?
choices: The traffic is placed in the priority queue at every hop
The switch re-marks the traffic by its own policy, so the PC gains nothing
The switch drops all EF traffic from that port
The switch converts the marking to CoS 5 only
questions.explanation: On an untrusted port the switch ignores incoming markings and applies its own classification and marking, commonly resetting to DSCP 0. That is the whole point of a trust boundary.

questions.question: The link in the exhibit is congested. How does the router treat the classes?
questions.code:
policy-map BRANCH-WAN
 class VOICE
  priority percent 10
 class CRITICAL-DATA
  bandwidth percent 40
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface Serial0/0/0
 bandwidth 10000
 service-policy output BRANCH-WAN
choices: CRITICAL-DATA is sent first because it has the larger percentage
VOICE is guaranteed at least 1 Mbps but waits its turn; CRITICAL-DATA is capped at 4 Mbps
VOICE is always sent first but capped at about 1 Mbps; CRITICAL-DATA gets at least about 4 Mbps
All classes share the link equally because fair-queue is configured
questions.explanation: priority makes VOICE an LLQ priority queue, served first but policed to 10 percent of 10 Mbps during congestion. bandwidth gives CRITICAL-DATA a CBWFQ minimum of 40 percent, about 4 Mbps, not a cap. fair-queue applies only inside class-default.

questions.question: An IP phone is the trust boundary and a PC is plugged into the phone's PC port. What does the phone typically do with the PC's traffic?
choices: Re-marks it to a low value so the PC cannot claim voice priority
Marks it EF so it shares the voice queue
Drops it until the PC authenticates
Passes the PC's markings through unchanged
questions.explanation: Because the boundary is at the phone, the phone must not let the PC's own markings through. It re-marks PC traffic (typically CoS 0) while marking its own voice CoS 5 and DSCP EF.

questions.question: Which queuing tool always serves its priority queue first?
choices: CBWFQ
FIFO
WRED
LLQ
questions.explanation: LLQ adds a strict priority queue to CBWFQ; the scheduler always sends waiting priority packets next. WRED is congestion avoidance, not a scheduler.

questions.question: What does CBWFQ guarantee each class during congestion?
choices: A minimum share of the link bandwidth
Strict priority over all other classes
Zero packet loss for every class
A maximum delay of 150 ms
questions.explanation: CBWFQ uses weighted round robin so each class gets at least its configured share when the link is busy. Strict priority is LLQ, and neither tool can promise zero loss.

questions.question: LLQ's priority queue is configured with `priority percent 20`. During congestion, voice reaches 30 percent of the link. What happens?
choices: Voice takes 30 percent and the other classes share what is left
The extra voice is moved into class-default
Voice above 20 percent is dropped by the priority queue's built-in policer
The router raises the priority queue to 30 percent automatically
questions.explanation: The priority bandwidth is a cap during congestion, enforced by an implicit policer, so other queues are not starved. Excess voice is dropped, which is why priority queues must be sized for the expected calls.

questions.question: Which three are parts of a queuing system with multiple queues? (Choose three.)
choices: A classifier that picks the queue for each packet
The queues that hold waiting packets
A scheduler that picks the next packet to send
A policer on every queue
A trust boundary on the interface
questions.explanation: Classifier, queues and scheduler make up the queuing system. A policer is only built into the LLQ priority queue, and the trust boundary is a marking design decision.

questions.question: Voice must always be sent first, up to 20 percent of the link. What completes the configuration?
questions.code:
policy-map WAN-EDGE
 class VOICE
  _____ percent 20
 class BUSINESS
  bandwidth percent 40
 class class-default
  fair-queue
choices: bandwidth
priority
police
shape
questions.explanation: priority creates the LLQ priority queue for the class, capped at the given rate during congestion. bandwidth would give only a CBWFQ minimum share, and police or shape would limit the rate without priority treatment.

questions.question: What is tail drop?
choices: Discarding newly arriving packets because the queue is full
Dropping the oldest packet at the head of the queue
Dropping packets that exceed a policed rate
Discarding packets with a bad checksum
questions.explanation: With no congestion avoidance, a full queue has no room at its tail, so every new packet for it is discarded, whatever its importance.

questions.question: At what point does WRED start randomly dropping packets?
choices: When the average queue depth passes the minimum threshold
When the average queue depth passes the maximum threshold
When traffic exceeds the CIR
At the end of every Tc interval
questions.explanation: Between the minimum and maximum thresholds WRED drops a rising random share. Above the maximum it drops everything. CIR and Tc belong to policing and shaping.

questions.question: Why is WRED not applied to the queue carrying voice?
choices: WRED cannot read the DSCP EF value in voice packets
Voice queues never hold enough packets for WRED to act
Voice uses UDP, which does not back off after drops, so early drops only hurt calls
WRED works only on 802.1Q trunk links that carry CoS
questions.explanation: WRED relies on TCP senders backing off after a loss. Voice over UDP keeps sending at the same rate, so dropping it early just damages calls. Voice belongs in the LLQ priority queue instead.

questions.question: What is TCP global synchronization?
choices: TCP hosts aligning their clocks with an NTP server
Many TCP flows losing packets at once, then slowing and speeding up together
Every TCP flow on a link negotiating the same window size
Routers sharing TCP session state for fast failover
questions.explanation: Tail drop hits many flows at once, so they all cut their windows together, underuse the link, then ramp up together and overflow the queue again. WRED's early random drops break that pattern.

questions.question: What does a policer do with traffic above its configured rate?
choices: Queues it and sends it later
Compresses it
Sends it over a backup link
Drops it or re-marks it
questions.explanation: Policing drops the excess or re-marks it to a lower class. Queuing the excess for later is what a shaper does.

questions.question: Which statement about shaping is correct?
choices: It drops excess traffic immediately and works only on ingress
It queues excess traffic, adding delay, and works only on egress
It raises the physical speed of the link
It re-marks excess traffic to CS0
questions.explanation: A shaper holds excess packets in a queue and releases them at the shaping rate, so it adds delay but avoids most loss, and it applies to outgoing traffic only.

questions.question: A router shapes to 100 Mbps on a 1 Gbps interface using a 1-second Tc. Voice calls through it have long gaps. What should change?
choices: Increase Tc to 2 seconds
Replace shaping with WRED
Mark voice AF11 instead of EF
Shorten the shaping interval (Tc) to about 10 ms
questions.explanation: With a 1-second Tc the shaper sends for 100 ms and then pauses for 900 ms, so voice can wait far past its 150 ms budget. A 10 ms Tc limits that wait to a few milliseconds, and LLQ inside the shaper then sends voice first.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly compare policing and shaping? (Choose two.)
choices: Policing causes loss but adds no delay
Shaping adds delay but avoids most loss
Shaping is usually applied by the provider on ingress
Policing buffers excess traffic in a queue
Both increase the available bandwidth
questions.explanation: Police drops, shape delays. Providers police at ingress; customers shape at egress. Neither adds bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the difference between policing and shaping?
questions.answer: Both limit traffic to a configured rate. Policing drops or re-marks the excess immediately (loss, no added delay) and is typically used inbound, for example by a provider at the CIR. Shaping queues the excess and sends it later (delay, little loss) and works only outbound.
questions.explanation: A typical pairing: the customer shapes to the CIR so the provider's policer never drops anything.

questions.question: A provider applies the exhibit on the port facing a customer. What happens to the customer's traffic above 10 Mbps?
questions.code:
policy-map CUSTOMER-IN
 class class-default
  police 10000000 conform-action transmit exceed-action set-dscp-transmit cs1
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 service-policy input CUSTOMER-IN
choices: It is dropped immediately
It is queued and sent later at 10 Mbps
It is re-marked CS1 and forwarded, so it can be dropped first if the network is busy
It is moved into the priority queue
questions.explanation: This is a policer: conforming traffic is transmitted unchanged, and exceed-action set-dscp-transmit cs1 re-marks the excess to a low class and still forwards it. Nothing is queued, which is shaping, and a policer could drop the excess only if its exceed-action said drop.

questions.question: What does the policy in the exhibit do?
questions.code:
policy-map SHAPE-20M
 class class-default
  shape average 20000000
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 service-policy output SHAPE-20M
choices: Drops all traffic above 20 Mbps
Guarantees class-default at least 20 Mbps during congestion
Marks traffic above 20 Mbps CS1
Queues traffic above 20 Mbps and sends it later, smoothing the output to 20 Mbps
questions.explanation: shape average sets a shaping rate on outbound traffic: excess packets wait in the shaping queue and leave when the rate allows, adding delay instead of loss. Dropping or re-marking would be police, and a minimum guarantee would be bandwidth.

questions.question: An engineer tries to attach a policy containing `priority percent 20` with `service-policy input` on a WAN interface, and IOS refuses. Why?
choices: Queuing schedules packets waiting to leave an interface, so a priority queue only works in an output policy
priority requires the bandwidth command in the same class
Input policies can only match CoS, not DSCP
LLQ works only on 802.1Q trunk interfaces
questions.explanation: A device can only choose the order of packets it is about to transmit, so queuing tools (priority, bandwidth) and shaping belong in output policies. Input policies can classify, mark and police. priority does not need bandwidth, and LLQ works on any interface type.

questions.question: Softphone traffic must be marked as voice at the access switch. What completes the policy?
questions.code:
policy-map MARK-IN
 class SOFTPHONE
  _____ dscp ef
 class class-default
  set dscp default
choices: match
set
priority
police
questions.explanation: set dscp ef writes the EF value into the IP header of every packet in the class. match belongs in a class-map, priority creates a queue rather than a marking, and police limits a rate.

questions.question: Put the QoS actions in the order a branch phone's voice packet meets them on its way to headquarters.
items: The IP phone marks the packet DSCP EF
The access switch trusts the phone's marking at the trust boundary
Core switches queue it by its DSCP without classifying it again
The branch WAN router places it in the LLQ priority queue inside the shaper
The provider edge polices the branch's traffic at the CIR
questions.explanation: Marking happens once at the source, trust is decided at the first switch, every later hop acts on the DSCP, the branch router queues and shapes on egress, and the provider polices on ingress to its network.

questions.question: Which three header fields can carry a QoS marking? (Choose three.)
choices: DSCP in the IP header
CoS (PCP) in the 802.1Q tag
EXP bits in an MPLS label
TTL in the IP header
Source port in the UDP header
questions.explanation: DSCP (6 bits) lives in the IP header end to end, CoS (3 bits) in the 802.1Q tag on trunks, and EXP (3 bits) in MPLS labels inside a provider network; Wi-Fi uses the TID. TTL counts router hops, and ports identify applications but are not markings.

questions.question: What is the decimal DSCP value of CS6, the class selector commonly used for routing protocol traffic?
questions.explanation: Class selector values are 8 times the class number: CS6 = 8 x 6 = 48, binary 110000. Its first three bits, 110, equal IP Precedence 6.

questions.question: A packet capture shows the IPv4 ToS (DS) byte as 0x88. Which marking is that?
choices: AF41
CS4
AF42
EF
questions.explanation: 0x88 is 10001000. DSCP is the first six bits, 100010, which is 34, and 34 = 8 x 4 + 2 x 1, so AF41. The last two bits are ECN. CS4 would be 0x80, AF42 0x90 and EF 0xB8.

questions.question: Match each per-hop behavior tool to an example of it.

pairs.right: An ACL or NBAR identifies softphone traffic
set dscp ef writes a value into the IP header
WRED drops a few TCP segments early
The provider drops traffic above the CIR
The branch router buffers traffic to stay under the CIR

questions.explanation: These are the six blueprint terms for item 4.7. Classification decides what a packet is, marking records it, queuing and congestion avoidance decide order and early drops on a busy interface, and policing and shaping enforce a rate by dropping or by delaying.

questions.question: What is a QoS trust boundary?
questions.answer: The point in the network where QoS markings start to be trusted, ideally an access switch port or a Cisco IP phone that IT controls. Markings arriving from beyond it, such as from a user's PC, are ignored or rewritten.
questions.explanation: Without a trust boundary, any user could mark their traffic EF and compete with real voice in the priority queue.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode on the WAN interface. Type the command that applies policy map WAN-OUT to traffic leaving the interface.
questions.explanation: service-policy attaches a policy map to an interface in one direction. A shaping and queuing policy like WAN-OUT must be output, because queues only exist for packets waiting to be sent.
